title: A Few of the Benefits of Large Families
author: Michael Foster
summary: Foster catalogs substantive benefits of large families across three dimensions: childhood development, household longevity, and societal stability. He contends that siblings create a living laboratory for social skills, character formation through unavoidable friction, and natural resistance to entitlement—lessons only children must learn deliberately but large-family children acquire through daily practice. Over a lifetime, sibling relationships provide robust care networks, shared burden in aging parent care, and compound meaning that offsets the early stress. Societally, large families transmit culture, preserve tradition, and address demographic crises that low-fertility societies cannot solve through individual choice alone.
points: Siblings provide relentless, unavoidable training in self-control, conflict repair, and perspective-taking—lessons that reach adulthood as measurably higher interpersonal skill.
Character forms not in isolation but through ordinary friction: disappointment, inconvenience, shared resources, and negotiated schedules teach humility and frustration tolerance early.
Parental loneliness and eldercare burden distribute across healthy sibling networks, reducing isolation and crisis risk in ways research correlates with life satisfaction across the lifespan.

Large families function as institutional carriers of tradition and culture—meaning that compounds over time even as early-stage stress peaks, reversing the assumption that early sacrifice eliminates later reward.

Demographic stability is not optional: sustained low fertility creates predictable crises (labor shortages, pension collapse, care gaps) that large families, intentionally formed, help stabilize at the societal level.
quotes: If you're fully invested in it, a large family is a blessing: to your children, to your household, and to society. Not everyone can have this kind of family, and not everyone should.

Children with siblings live inside a constant negotiation. Who gets the seat. Who touched whose stuff. Who's lying. Who's sulking. Who needs to apologize. They learn, whether they want to or not, how to read moods, repair conflict, wait their turn, and restrain themselves.
Large families are loud. Disappointing. Inconvenient. Someone is always in your way. This provides a lot of training. Kids learn to absorb frustration without melting down because they have to.

When sibling relationships are healthy, they tend to stay that way. The research shows lower loneliness and stronger relational stability well into adulthood. Only children are far more likely to face eldercare alone: emotionally, financially, logistically.

Traditions stick when there are enough people to carry them. Stories survive when more than one child remembers them. Sociologically speaking, large families behave and perform more like institutions. And institutions, unlike individuals, can endure.

Societies with sustained low fertility don't drift gently into decline. They hit predictable walls: labor shortages, care crises, pension collapse, cultural fragmentation.” Archived from We Made People (Foster Substack) on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
